question: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of severe lower back pain for the past 2 days. The pain is constant and non-radiating, and he describes it as 7 out of 10 in intensity. The pain began after he helped a friend move into a new apartment. Three weeks ago, he was diagnosed with urethritis and was treated with azithromycin and ceftriaxone. He has a history of intravenous heroin use. He takes no medications. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 128/90 mm Hg. Examination shows old track marks on the cubital fossae bilaterally. His lumbar paraspinal muscles are firm and tense on palpation. There is no midline spinal tenderness. Flexing the hip and extending the knee while raising the leg to 70° does not cause any pain. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: History of intravenous heroin use -> increased risk of infectious complications -> possible spinal infection -> 60% CHAIN: Severe lower back pain after physical exertion -> consider musculoskeletal injury -> 70% CHAIN: Lumbar paraspinal muscles firm and tense on palpation -> suggestive of muscle strain -> 80% CHAIN: No midline spinal tenderness -> less likely to be a spinal cord issue -> 90% CHAIN: Flexing hip and extending knee without pain -> negative straight leg raise test -> less likely to be disc herniation -> 90% CHAIN: Urinalysis showing no abnormalities -> less likely to be related to genitourinary infection -> 90% CHAIN: Considering the patient's history and physical exam findings, the most appropriate next step is analgesia and regular activity -> 60%
analysis: The patient's presentation with lower back pain, history of urethritis, intravenous drug use, and lack of specific findings on physical exam make ankylosing spondylitis less likely. The absence of red flags for serious spinal pathology suggests a musculoskeletal etiology. Given the recent history of heavy lifting, the most appropriate next step would be to provide analgesia and encourage regular activity to manage acute mechanical low back pain.
